issues.legal_issue: A court may enlarge the time for filing a certified copy in an appeal when it has permitted the copy to be filed later, and should not dismiss the appeal without considering that power.
material_facts: The execution second appeal was filed without a certified copy of the challenged order.
At admission, the High Court permitted the copy to be filed as soon as it became available.
The appellant obtained the copy and filed it seven days later, and also applied for condonation of delay.
The High Court dismissed the appeal as time-barred without considering its power to enlarge time under Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in dismissing the appeal without considering and exercising its discretionary power under Section 148; the appeal was allowed and the High Court's order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers a court, in its discretion, to enlarge a period fixed or granted by the court for an act prescribed or allowed by the Code, even after that period has expired. The power is to be used when necessary to secure the ends of justice. Section 5 of the Limitation Act was also invoked by the appellant, and the Court found no reason why the delay could not be condoned. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.execution_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from an execution matter.
predicates.court_allowed_later_filing_of_required_c: The court permitted the appellant to file a required copy after the appeal was presented.
predicates.copy_filed_promptly_after_becoming_avail: The appellant filed the copy soon after obtaining it.

issues.definition: When an execution appeal is presented without a required copy, but the court permits later filing and the appellant files it promptly after it becomes available, the appeal should not be dismissed without considering extension of time.

issues.legal_issue: A court may accept a small, bona fide shortfall in a timely deposit under a pre-emption decree when the shortfall is later made good.
material_facts: A decree in a pre-emption suit required the decree-holder to deposit the purchase money and costs by a specified date.
The decree-holder deposited nearly all of the required amount by that date, but the deposit was short by 25 paise because of a bona fide mistake.
The decree-holder later deposited the shortfall with the executing court's permission.
The executing court accepted the late shortfall, but the execution appellate court treated the decree as dismissed and refused to condone the default.
issues.conclusion: The delayed shortfall should have been accepted in the exercise of discretion under Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure; the Supreme Court restored the executing court's order.
issues.legal_principle: Order XX, Rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires a decree-holder in a pre-emption suit to deposit the purchase money and any decreed costs by the date fixed by the court. Section 148 empowers the court to enlarge a period fixed by it, even after it has expired, in its discretion and to secure the ends of justice. In the circumstances, the small shortfall resulted from a bona fide mistake, and refusing to accept the later payment would deprive the decree-holder of the fruits of the decree. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.preemption_decree_execution: The proceeding concerns execution of a decree granting pre-emption.
predicates.purchase_money_and_costs_mostly_deposite: The decree-holder deposited nearly all of the purchase money and decreed costs by the court's deadline.
predicates.small_shortfall_caused_by_bona_fide_mist: A small part of the required deposit was omitted because of a bona fide mistake.
predicates.shortfall_later_paid: The decree-holder later paid the omitted amount.

issues.definition: When execution of a pre-emption decree involves a timely deposit that falls short by a small amount through bona fide mistake, and the shortfall is later paid, the court should accept the delayed shortfall.
